title: Culapanthaka's white cloth
hook: a slow monk rubs a white cloth until it's gray and understands (Dhammapada 25 story)

segments.voice: Yesterday: sukha, ease on frozen leaves, with nothing left burning. Your line: I sleep well. Today, a monk who couldn't learn one verse.

One verse. That's all the young monk Culapanthaka has to learn, and it won't stay. The Dhammapada commentary tells how he tries and tries, and every new line pushes out the one before. His older brother, Mahapanthaka, an accomplished monk, finally gives up on him and tells him to go home. So early one morning Culapanthaka stands at the monastery gate, in tears, ready to leave. The Buddha meets him there, takes him by the hand, and leads him back inside. Today, what the Buddha hands him.
screen: `ONE VERSE WON'T STAY.` → `GO HOME, SAYS HIS BROTHER.` → `THE BUDDHA AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: First, the cloth. Not another verse. The Buddha gives him a clean white cloth, and tells him to sit and rub it with his hand, repeating a short phrase: removing dirt, removing dirt. Second, the change. As he rubs, the clean cloth slowly grows soiled. The commentary says he saw it plainly: this cloth was pure white, and now, because of this body, it's dirty. Things change. Third, the inner cloth. Then the Buddha speaks to him about the real dirt: not dust, but greed, hatred and delusion. Those are what a monk removes. The commentary says Culapanthaka understood, right there, and became an arahant. Fourth, the meal. That same day, the story goes on, the physician Jivaka, the doctor of three days ago, had invited the Buddha and the monks to his house. Mahapanthaka, who arranged the invitations, had left his slow brother out. The Buddha wouldn't begin until Culapanthaka was sent for. And the commentary attaches a Dhammapada verse to his story: by rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and self-control, the wise one makes an island no flood can sweep away. The slow monk didn't get there by memorizing. He got there with a cloth, his own two hands, and a teacher who met him at the gate. The cloth grows gray.
screen: `A WHITE CLOTH, NOT A VERSE.` · `THE CLEAN CLOTH GROWS SOILED.` · `THE REAL DIRT IS INSIDE.` · `SENT FOR, AT JIVAKA'S MEAL.` · then, large: `THE CLOTH GROWS GRAY.`

segments.voice: If there's a cloth nearby, a napkin, a dish towel, a sleeve, take it in your hands; if not, use the hem of your shirt. Rub it slowly between your fingers, feel the weave, and notice that your hands are already leaving something on it: warmth, a little oil, a crease. Nothing stays exactly as it was.
Rajoharana, removing dirt. The phrase the Buddha gave Culapanthaka to repeat while rubbing a clean cloth until it was soiled. Today's word.
Your line: the cloth grows gray. Slow to memorize didn't mean slow to see. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Teachers in Buddhist communities retell Culapanthaka's story to encourage students who learn slowly, and in some monasteries cleaning and sweeping are themselves treated as mindfulness practice.

chat.says: I'm a slow learner. Did slow students ever get anywhere in the Buddha's time?
options: Culapanthaka couldn't learn one verse, yet with a cloth he saw and woke.
No, a monk who couldn't memorize verses was always sent home.
Only after he memorized every verse, the way his brother had.
chat.meaning: The Buddha gave Culapanthaka a white cloth instead of a verse. Watching it soil, he saw that things change, and became an arahant.

notes: Commentary story paraphrased. Confirm: the verse he couldn't learn (the time spent, given in months, is omitted); Mahapanthaka telling him to leave; the Buddha meeting him at the gate and taking him by the hand; the clean white cloth and the phrase 'rajoharanam' (removal of dirt); his insight into impermanence; the Buddha's verses on lust, hatred and delusion as the real dust; arahantship; Jivaka's invitation, Mahapanthaka as the one arranging invitations, and the Buddha waiting until Culapanthaka was fetched. The psychic display at Jivaka's house is omitted.

Dhammapada 25 paraphrased; Max Muller 1881 ('By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm') could be quoted if a Keeper confirms the exact wording.
'From three days ago' refers to day 769 (Jivaka).
